newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - MPT unit HK Tel loan expected.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - MPT unit HK Tel loan expected.

text.p: A unit of China Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT) may follow the trail blazed by a rival telecommunications provider and borrow money to buy into Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd, bankers said on Monday.
Bankers expect the unit, China Telecom (Hong Kong), to seek finance from banks to help fund its Hongkong Telecom stake.
"We want to be involved," said one senior banker, bidding for a mandate for a three-year loan of about US$800 million from China Telecom (Hong Kong).
"The industry is an industry which has no credit problems. Telecoms are a very strong and robust industry," he said.
Bankers want relationships with MPT, effectively a sovereign risk.
Earlier this month, China Telecom agreed to buy 5.5 percent of Hongkong Telecom at HK$14.25 a share, a total of HK$9.177 billion.
They said the deal would probably resemble the fundraising by a unit of China Everbright Holdings Co Ltd, which last month took 7.74 percent of Hongkong Telecom.
Earlier this month, a unit of China Everbright Holdings Co Ltd, controlled by China's State Council, signed a US$1.05 billion loan to part-fund its Hongkong Telecom stake.
An arranger group has formed for Bakrie Indonesia BV's US$125 million guaranteed floating rate notes due 2001, which was officially launched on Monday.

Arrangers and lead managers are Sumitomo Finance (Asia), (books), Bear Stearns Asia, Credit Lyonnais, Dong Ah Securities, Natwest Markets, Overseas Union Bank, Pt Bank Internasional Indonesia and Union Bank of Switzerland Hong Kong branch.
Korea Development Bank set its US$300 milliion five-year floating rate note in London on Monday.
Margin was 18.75 basis points over three-month London Interbank Offered Rate, and issue price was 99.95.
Callable at par after three years, the notes include a put on coupon dates if the ratings fall below either A3/A-minus.
The loan sector continues to be more active and interesting than the rest of the market, which is languishing, partly because yields are becoming too tight for investors' tastes.
Banks said swap rates are too tight, making it difficult to get an issue away.
"I think one of the problems is absolute yield," said one banker active in the Hong Kong dollar market.
"Yields even on floating-rate paper are getting very tight. We're seeing yields at a quarter (of a percentage point) over one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate," he said.
